reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO laboratory manual for semen analysis
clinicalPearls: Azoospermia is the complete absence of sperm from the ejaculate confirmed after centrifugation of at least two properly collected samples

The obstructive form features intact spermatogenesis blocked from reaching the ejaculate, so the testes are of normal size and consistency and follicle-stimulating hormone is characteristically normal
This combination of normal testicular volume with normal follicle-stimulating hormone is the key clinical discriminator from the non-obstructive form
A low semen volume with an acidic, fructose-negative sample suggests distal obstruction at the ejaculatory ducts or absence of the vasa and seminal vesicles
Causes include vasal or epididymal obstruction from prior infection or surgery, previous vasectomy, ejaculatory duct obstruction, and congenital absence of the vas deferens
Palpable absence of the vasa mandates cystic-fibrosis gene testing of the man and his partner because of the risk to offspring
Sperm can almost always be retrieved surgically from the epididymis or testis for use with intracytoplasmic sperm injection, and selected cases are amenable to reconstructive surgery
Scrotal and transrectal ultrasound help localise the level of obstruction and detect dilated seminal vesicles or ejaculatory duct cysts
reference.pathophysiology: In obstructive azoospermia sperm production within the seminiferous tubules is preserved, but a mechanical blockage anywhere along the excurrent pathway, from the epididymis through the vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory ducts, prevents sperm from entering the ejaculate. Because the pituitary-testicular axis and germ-cell production are intact, follicle-stimulating hormone and testicular volume remain normal. Obstruction may be congenital, as in bilateral absence of the vas deferens linked to cystic-fibrosis gene mutations, or acquired through infection, iatrogenic injury, prior vasectomy, or ejaculatory duct obstruction from cysts or calculi. When the distal ducts or seminal vesicles are involved, ejaculate volume falls and fructose, a seminal-vesicle product, is reduced or absent.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
Ejaculatory duct obstruction from a cyst or calculus
Retrograde ejaculation or failure of emission producing an empty antegrade ejaculate
additionalInvestigations: Repeat centrifuged semen analysis with assessment of volume, pH, and fructose
Serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, and testosterone, expected to be normal in true obstruction
Scrotal ultrasound to assess the testes and epididymis and detect dilated tubules
Transrectal ultrasound to identify ejaculatory duct obstruction, seminal-vesicle dilatation, or midline cysts
Cystic-fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene testing when the vasa are absent or distal obstruction is found
Post-ejaculatory urine analysis to exclude a retrograde component
Diagnostic testicular sampling to confirm intact spermatogenesis where doubt remains
redFlags: Palpable absence of the vasa deferentia requiring genetic counselling before conception
A midline prostatic or ejaculatory duct cyst amenable to targeted treatment
Associated renal anomaly on imaging, which may accompany unilateral vasal agenesis
Features suggesting the azoospermia is in fact non-obstructive, altering the retrieval strategy
reference.prognosis: The reproductive outlook is generally favourable because spermatogenesis is intact, so surgical sperm retrieval combined with intracytoplasmic sperm injection has high success, and selected acquired obstructions can be reconstructed with restoration of sperm in the ejaculate.
pitfalls: Labelling a man azoospermic without examining a centrifuged specimen on more than one occasion
Failing to check ejaculate volume, pH, and fructose, which localise distal obstruction
Omitting cystic-fibrosis gene testing when the vasa are impalpable
Confusing obstructive with non-obstructive azoospermia by not integrating testicular volume with follicle-stimulating hormone
Overlooking retrograde ejaculation as a cause of an apparently empty ejaculate
references: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen
European Association of Urology guidelines on sexual and reproductive health
management: Restore the excurrent pathway where feasible with microsurgical vasovasostomy or vasoepididymostomy for vasal or epididymal obstruction, or transurethral resection of the ejaculatory ducts for ductal obstruction

Where reconstruction is not possible or unsuccessful, retrieve sperm surgically by percutaneous or microsurgical epididymal aspiration or testicular sperm extraction for intracytoplasmic sperm injection
Cryopreserve retrieved spermatozoa to allow assisted-reproduction cycles without repeated procedures
Offer CFTR mutation testing of the man and his partner before treatment when the vasa are absent, with genetic counselling on transmission risk to offspring
Treat any reversible contributory factor such as previous genital tract infection, managing the couple jointly with a reproductive medicine and embryology team
Refer for assisted-conception counselling covering success rates and the option of donor sperm
